content: Hydrops fetalis is a critical medical condition characterized by the accumulation of abnormal amounts of fluid in at least two or more body compartments of a fetus or newborn. Symptoms of Hydrops Fetalis: The symptoms vary depending on the severity of the condition. In mild cases, symptoms may include: Swelling of the liver. Pale skin (pallor). In more severe cases, symptoms may include: Respiratory distress or difficulty breathing. Bruising or purplish bruise-like spots on the skin. Heart failure. Severe anemia. Severe jaundice. Generalized swelling of the entire body. Causes of Hydrops Fetalis: There are two main types of hydrops fetalis: immune and non-immune. Immune hydrops fetalis is a complication of severe Rh incompatibility. This condition leads to massive destruction of red blood cells, resulting in complications such as total body swelling. The swelling can impair the function of vital organs. Non-immune hydrops fetalis occurs when a disease or medical condition disrupts the body’s ability to regulate fluid. The primary causes of this type include: Cardiac or pulmonary issues. Severe anemia, such as that caused by thalassemia. Genetic abnormalities, including Turner syndrome. The incidence of immune hydrops fetalis has significantly decreased due to the use of Rh immunoglobulin (RhoGAM), a medication administered to pregnant women at risk for Rh incompatibility. Diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound may reveal: Excessive amniotic fluid (polyhydramnios). An abnormally large placenta. Fluid accumulation causing swelling in the fetus’s abdominal area and organs, such as the liver, spleen, heart, or lungs. Amniocentesis and frequent ultrasounds are often performed to assess the severity of the condition. Treatment Options: Treatment depends on the underlying cause. During pregnancy, options may include: Administration of medication to induce early labor and delivery. Early cesarean delivery if the condition worsens. Intrauterine fetal blood transfusion to provide red blood cells to the fetus. For newborns, treatment may involve: Direct transfusion of packed red blood cells compatible with the infant’s blood type, along with exchange transfusion to remove harmful substances destroying red blood cells. Removal of excess fluid from around the lungs or abdominal area using a needle. Medications to manage heart failure and support kidney function in removing excess fluids. Respiratory support, such as mechanical ventilation, to assist with breathing. Prognosis: Hydrops fetalis often results in the death of the infant shortly before or after delivery. The risk of mortality is highest among extremely premature infants and those who are critically ill at birth. Complications: A potential complication is kernicterus, a form of brain damage caused by severe jaundice. Prevention: Rh incompatibility, a preventable cause of hydrops fetalis, can be avoided if the mother receives Rh immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) at specific times during and after pregnancy.
